analysis.one_liner: Guarantees health benefits for retired coal miners whose companies shut down, funded by premiums on coal producers and importers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 43 sponsors and cosponsors but was referred to two House committees in November 1991 and never received a vote; it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: When coal companies go out of business, their retired miners can lose promised health coverage. This bill would have created a government-chartered corporation to pay medical and death benefits for those retirees and their widows and dependents, funded by a 75-cent-per-hour premium on coal production work, a 15-cent-per-ton premium on imported coal, and annual per-beneficiary premiums from the companies last bound to the union wage agreements. It also would have merged several struggling union health plans into a new self-funded benefit fund.
analysis.who_benefits: 'Orphan miners' — retired coal miners whose employer closed or left the industry — plus their spouses, surviving spouses and dependents, who would get medical and death benefits at levels matching their old plans. Retirees still covered by solvent companies would keep those guarantees as long as the company stays in business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired coal miners and their widows

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Coal Industry Retiree Health Benefit Corporation to provide medical and death benefits to orphan miners, their spouses, surviving spouses and dependents.
Funds the program through an hourly premium of 75 cents on each hour of coal production work, a per-ton premium on imported coal, and annual per-beneficiary premiums from last signatory operators.
Merges excess assets from closed coal-industry plans into a new United Mine Workers of America 1991 Benefit Fund, with eligibility rules for retirees of signatory operators.
Requires the last signatory operator of anyone receiving retiree health benefits as of February 1, 1993 to keep providing those benefits for as long as it remains in business.
The bill's findings state that withdrawals of contributing employers from the union benefit plans raised funding burdens for remaining employers and impaired health care for retirees.

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers, via the hourly premium on every hour of coal production work; importers of foreign coal, via a 15-cent-per-ton premium; and the union-signatory companies still in business, which must keep covering their own retirees and pay annual per-beneficiary premiums for miners they once employed. Some of these costs could be passed on in coal prices.

drawbacks.text: The premiums are a mandatory tax on all coal production and imports, which coal companies could pass along to utilities and consumers in the price of coal.
Benefit levels are capped at what retirees' old plans provided and cannot exceed them, so the bill guarantees coverage but not richer benefits.

The bill mandates managed care rules — drug formularies, utilization review, and payments to doctors capped at Medicare allowable charges — which restrict beneficiaries' choice of providers and how care is delivered, even while barring balance billing of patients.

Last signatory operators are locked into providing retiree benefits 'for as long as the last signatory operator remains in business,' with a broad definition of staying in business that reaches into corporate control groups, creating an open-ended liability that could deter companies from signing union wage agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — that retirees of bankrupt coal companies keep their health coverage — is real and funded by premiums on the industry that made the promises, not by general taxpayers. The honest cost is that the funding falls on every coal producer and importer and may show up in coal prices, and the open-ended obligation on companies that once signed union agreements is heavy and could discourage future signatories. On balance it is a targeted, industry-funded fix to a genuine retirement-benefit crisis, not a badly designed bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, routed to a Labor-Management Relations subcommittee a month later, and neither committee ever reported it out, so it simply expired when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 26, 1991 by Rep. John Murtha with five original cosponsors and referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Education and Labor.
It drew 42 additional cosponsors — 39 Democrats, 2 Republicans and 1 Independent.
On December 30, 1991 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and no further action was ever recorded.
No roll-call vote was ever taken on the bill in either chamber before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers and importers avoided the new hourly and per-ton premiums, and union-signatory companies avoided the open-ended retiree benefit obligations and per-beneficiary premiums. Retired miners whose companies had shut down went on waiting for a fix, which Congress did not enact from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal companies that would have paid the premiums

for.name: Rep. John P. Murtha
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with five original cosponsors from coal-mining districts and championed retiree health protections.

for.name: 42 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 39 Democrats, 2 Republicans and 1 Independent.

for.name: Reps. Mollohan, Rahall, Staggers, Wise and McCloskey
for.what_they_did: Joined Murtha as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions funding the program
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 26, 1991 and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over benefit plans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 26, 1991 and referred it to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, where it died without a markup or vote.

against.name: Coal industry employers
against.what_they_did: The bill's premiums and open-ended retiree obligations fell on coal producers and importers; no industry lobbying campaign appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 39 of the 42 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans and 1 Independent — and since the bill never reached a floor vote, no roll call ever recorded where the parties stood.

industries.note: Every producer would pay a 75-cent premium on each hour of coal production work, and signatory companies would owe annual per-beneficiary premiums and continuing retiree benefits. The industry's savings from shedding these obligations came directly out of retired miners' health coverage.
A 15-cent-per-ton premium on imported coal was imposed to keep imports from undercutting the domestic funding base.

industries.industry: Health care providers and managed care networks
industries.note: The bill routes benefits through managed care networks with drug formularies and utilization review, guaranteeing a patient volume, but caps physician payments at Medicare allowable charges and bars balance billing, which limits provider revenue.
